report:
Based on my research, your suspicion is correct — the overall evidence does **not** support ginkgo extract as an effective treatment for tinnitus.

**Key evidence:**

1. **Cochrane Review (2013):** The most authoritative assessment, published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, included four trials with 1,543 participants. It concluded there was **no reliable evidence** that ginkgo biloba reduces tinnitus severity compared to placebo. ([Cochrane](https://www.cochrane.org/hr/evidence/CD003852_ginkgo-biloba-tinnitus))

2. **Medwave summary:** Based on four randomized trials totaling 1,246 patients, ginkgo biloba **does not reduce the intensity of tinnitus or improve quality of life**. ([Medwave](https://www.medwave.cl/puestadia/resepis/7295.html?_view=en))

3. **Systematic review (Tandfonline):** A systematic review of randomized, placebo-controlled trials found mixed results depending on extract quality. A meta-analysis by Rejali et al., which pooled studies using various ginkgo products of differing quality, concluded that **ginkgo biloba does not benefit patients with tinnitus**. ([Tandfonline](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.2147/NDT.S22793))

4. **Double-blind placebo-controlled trial:** An early well-designed study found that ginkgo extract LI 1370 had **no greater therapeutic effect than placebo** in treating tinnitus. ([PMC/NIH](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC26593/))

**Why the confusion?** Some smaller, lower-quality studies and open-label trials (particularly using the standardized EGb 761 extract) have reported modest benefits, creating mixed signals. However, when high-quality randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews are considered, the consensus is that ginkgo extract is **no more effective than placebo** for tinnitus relief.
